title: Legal Assistant Resume Example & Writing Guide (2026)
meta_description: A complete legal assistant resume example with section-by-section guidance, 40+ legal skills, ATS keyword tips, and the mistakes that cost interviews.
content_html:
A legal assistant resume has a harder job than most. It has to prove you can do precise, high-stakes work — docketing, discovery, calendaring, client intake — while surviving the applicant tracking systems law firms use to filter candidates. Attorneys scan for specifics: which practice areas, which tools, how many cases, what deadlines you owned.

This guide gives you a full annotated example, a section-by-section breakdown, the skills and keywords legal hiring managers search for, and the mistakes that quietly cost interviews.

What Legal Hiring Managers Actually Look For

Ask an attorney what they want from a legal assistant and you won't hear "team player." You'll hear:

  • Practice-area fit. Litigation, corporate, family law, real estate, immigration — each has its own vocabulary and workflows. A resume that names the right one beats a generic one every time.
  • Proof you can handle deadlines. Statutes of limitations, court filing deadlines, discovery cutoffs. Your bullets should show you owned calendaring and docketing, not just "assisted with" them.
  • Tool fluency. Westlaw, LexisNexis, Relativity, Concordance, Clio, MyCase, PACER, e-filing systems. Firms search their applicant databases by these terms.
  • Discretion and client contact. Legal assistants see privileged information and often serve as the client's first point of contact. Evidence of trust matters.

If your resume reads like it could belong to any administrative assistant, it will lose to one that reads like a legal assistant.

Legal Assistant Resume Example

Below is a complete example for a mid-level litigation legal assistant. It's fictional — the names and firms are illustrative — but every bullet follows the pattern real hiring managers respond to: what you did, the scale, and the result.

DANA REYES
Denver, CO · (303) 555-0147 · dana.reyes@email.com

SUMMARY
Legal assistant with 6 years supporting litigation teams in civil defense. Managed discovery for 40+ active matters, maintained attorney calendars across 3 time zones, and e-filed 200+ pleadings with a 100% acceptance rate. Proficient in Relativity, Westlaw, and Clio.

SKILLS
Litigation support · E-discovery (Relativity, Concordance) · Legal research (Westlaw, LexisNexis) · Docketing & calendaring · E-filing (state & federal) · Discovery responses · Trial preparation · Deposition summaries · Client intake · Billing & time entry (Clio) · Document management · Proofreading & cite-checking

PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE

Legal Assistant — Hartwell & Marsh LLP, Denver, CO | 2021–Present

  • Coordinate discovery for 40+ active civil litigation matters, tracking deadlines in Clio and flagging conflicts 30 days out
  • Prepare and e-file 200+ pleadings, motions, and discovery responses in Colorado state and federal courts with a 100% acceptance rate
  • Summarize 50+ depositions (averaging 300 pages each) into 5-page attorney briefs within 48 hours of transcript receipt
  • Manage calendars for 4 attorneys, scheduling depositions, mediations, and court appearances across 3 time zones
  • Serve as first point of contact for 60+ clients, conducting intake interviews and maintaining privilege protocols

Legal Secretary — Brennan Legal Group, Denver, CO | 2018–2021

  • Supported 2 partners in family law practice; drafted correspondence, pleadings, and settlement documents
  • Maintained docketing system for 25 matters, zero missed deadlines over 3 years
  • Processed client billing and trust account entries, reconciling $180K in monthly receivables

EDUCATION
A.A.S., Paralegal Studies — Community College of Denver, 2018

CERTIFICATIONS
Certified Legal Assistant (CLA), NALA — 2020

Section-by-Section Breakdown

Summary: name the practice area and the proof

The example summary does four things in three sentences: names the specialty (litigation), gives years, quantifies the workload (40+ matters, 200+ filings), and names the tools. Compare that with the typical weak opener — "Detail-oriented legal assistant with strong organizational skills seeking a challenging position" — which says nothing a firm can verify or search for.

If you're entry-level, swap the years for your strongest asset: "Paralegal Studies graduate (A.A.S., 2026) with internship experience in personal injury intake and e-filing; NALA CLA candidate." New graduates get hired on education and demonstrated initiative, so lead with both.

Skills: group them like a recruiter searches

Notice the skills section groups by function, not alphabetically: litigation support tools, research platforms, docketing, trial work, billing. Recruiters search their ATS by these exact terms — "Relativity," "e-filing," "deposition summaries" — so a skills section written in the firm's own vocabulary is a keyword match before a human ever reads the page. Add both the acronym and the full name at least once ("e-discovery (Relativity)") since searchers use both.

Experience: own the verbs, show the stakes

The strongest pattern in legal bullets is action verb + legal task + scale + outcome:

Weak: "Responsible for filing documents."
Strong: "Prepare and e-file 200+ pleadings, motions, and discovery responses in Colorado state and federal courts with a 100% acceptance rate."

Quantify what you can: number of matters, attorneys supported, pages summarized, deadlines met. Where you can't quantify, quantify the inputs: "maintained docketing system for 25 matters" is stronger than any adjective.

Education and certifications: put them where they earn

For legal assistants, the NALA Certified Legal Assistant (CLA/CP) credential and NALS certifications carry real weight — hiring managers recognize and filter on them. List them in their own section, never buried inside education. Pursuing one? Say so: "CLA candidate, exam scheduled August 2026" signals seriousness.

The Legal Skills That Get You Found

Build your skills section from these groups, keeping only what you've actually done — claiming "Relativity" when you've never opened it will surface in the interview, not the search:

Litigation: e-discovery, document review, deposition summaries, trial preparation, exhibit management, witness coordination, subpoena preparation, discovery responses and objections

Research & writing: Westlaw, LexisNexis, legal research memoranda, cite-checking, proofreading, Bluebook citation, drafting pleadings and motions, correspondence

Case management: docketing, calendaring, deadline tracking, conflict checks, case file organization, Clio, MyCase, PracticePanther, document management systems

Court & filing: e-filing (state and federal), PACER, court rules and procedures, service of process coordination, notary public

Client & office: client intake interviews, privilege and confidentiality protocols, billing and time entry, trust accounting basics, scheduling across time zones, Spanish or other language fluency (a genuine differentiator in many markets)

Mirror the posting's exact phrasing for the top 5–10 terms. If the posting says "docket management" and you wrote "docketing," use both — the person who wrote the posting is the person whose search terms matter.

5 Mistakes That Cost Legal Assistants Interviews

  1. Reading like a generic admin. "Answered phones, scheduled appointments, filed documents" could describe a dental receptionist. Every bullet needs at least one legal-specific term.
  2. Hiding the practice area. Name your area in the summary and repeat it in bullets — a litigation firm assumes an unmarked resume needs training.
  3. No confidentiality signal. One bullet about maintaining privilege protocols reassures in a way "trustworthy" never does.
  4. Burying certifications. The CLA/CP is one of the few credentials attorneys filter on. If it's in small type at the bottom, you're hiding your best keyword.
  5. A format the firm's ATS can't parse. Many firms still run older parsing software. Single column, standard headings (Summary, Skills, Professional Experience, Education), real text — no text boxes, no graphics-based skill bars. FAQ

How long should a legal assistant resume be? One page for most legal assistants, including those with up to about 8 years of experience. Two pages is reasonable for senior legal assistants supporting partners across multiple practice areas — cut the oldest roles first, never the certifications.

Do legal assistants need a cover letter? Most firms still expect one, especially smaller and mid-size practices. Keep it to three short paragraphs: the role and why this firm, two sentences of proof (matters handled, tools, a result), and a close. Don't repeat the resume — add the motivation.

What is the most important skill on a legal assistant resume? Deadline ownership. Firms can train software; they can't train reliability. Bullets showing you managed dockets, calendaring, and filing deadlines without misses are the single most persuasive content on the page.

Should I list every software I've used? List what you can actually use and what the target role mentions. A skills section with 20 tools you touched once reads as padding; 6–10 you're fluent in reads as competence. Match the posting's terms exactly for the most important ones.

Does the CLA certification matter for legal assistant jobs? Yes — it's one of the few credentials hiring managers actively filter for. NALA's Certified Legal Assistant / Certified Paralegal and NALS certifications (ALS, PLS) are the recognized ones. List the credential in its own section, and note candidacy if you're pursuing it.

Can I use the same resume for paralegal and legal assistant roles? Not quite. Paralegal postings emphasize substantive legal work (research memos, drafting, case analysis); legal assistant postings emphasize support operations (calendaring, filing, intake, billing). Tailor the summary and the first three bullets to whichever role you're applying for — the 15 minutes of tailoring is worth more than a second generic version.
